claim: Closed-loop neuronal stimulation has a strong therapeutic potential for neurological disorders such as Parkinson's disease.
source: Closed-loop neuronal stimulation has a strong therapeutic potential for neurological disorders such as Parkinson's disease.
evidence: This is a general statement about the therapeutic potential of closed-loop stimulation, drawing from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Standard stimulation protocols rely on continuous open-loop stimulation.
source: However, at the moment, standard stimulation protocols rely on continuous open-loop stimulation and the design of adaptive controllers is an active field of research.
evidence: This describes the current state of stimulation protocols in the field.

claim: Delayed feedback control (DFC) has been proposed as a closed-loop technique for desynchronisation of neuronal populations.
source: Delayed feedback control (DFC), a popular method used to control chaotic systems, has been proposed as a closed-loop technique for desynchronisation of neuronal populations but, so far, was only tested in computational studies.
evidence: This statement references prior proposals in the literature about DFC applications.

claim: DFC was only tested in computational studies prior to this work.
source: Delayed feedback control (DFC), a popular method used to control chaotic systems, has been proposed as a closed-loop technique for desynchronisation of neuronal populations but, so far, was only tested in computational studies.
evidence: This claim establishes the novelty of the current work by stating what has been done previously.

claim: This work implements DFC for the first time in neuronal populations.
source: We implement DFC for the first time in neuronal populations and access its efficacy in disrupting unwanted neuronal oscillations.
evidence: This is a primary claim about the novelty of the experimental work presented.

claim: Conventional DFC worsens the neuronal population oscillatory behaviour.
source: We show that the conventional DFC in fact worsens the neuronal population oscillatory behaviour, which was never reported before.
evidence: This is a key finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The worsening of oscillatory behaviour by conventional DFC was never reported before.
source: We show that the conventional DFC in fact worsens the neuronal population oscillatory behaviour, which was never reported before.
evidence: This claim establishes the novelty of the finding by comparing to prior literature.

claim: Adaptive DFC (aDFC) monitors the ongoing oscillation periodicity and self-tunes accordingly.
source: Conversely, we present an improved control algorithm, adaptive DFC (aDFC), which monitors the ongoing oscillation periodicity and self-tunes accordingly.
evidence: This describes the design and functionality of the aDFC algorithm developed in this work.

claim: aDFC effectively disrupts collective neuronal oscillations restoring a more physiological state.
source: aDFC effectively disrupts collective neuronal oscillations restoring a more physiological state.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental results.

claim: aDFC is a better candidate for therapeutic closed-loop brain stimulation.
source: Overall, these results support aDFC as a better candidate for therapeutic closed-loop brain stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings comparing aDFC to other methods.

claim: Excessive oscillatory synchronisation emerges in neurological disorders such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy.
source: The excessive oscillatory synchronisation that emerges in neurological disorders, such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy (Uhlhaas and Singer, 2006), can be disrupted using direct electrical stimulation (Edwards et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Excessive oscillatory synchronisation can be disrupted using direct electrical stimulation.
source: The excessive oscillatory synchronisation that emerges in neurological disorders, such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy (Uhlhaas and Singer, 2006), can be disrupted using direct electrical stimulation (Edwards et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Edwards et al., 2017.

claim: Conventional brain stimulation therapies rely on continuous open-loop stimulation, leading to excessive stimulation and burdensome side-effects.
source: Despite its potential, conventional brain stimulation, therapies still rely on continuous open-loop stimulation, leading to excessive stimulation and burdensome side-effects (Kuo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kuo et al., 2018.

claim: Closed-loop stimulation guided by an efficient control algorithm should provide better outcomes, disrupting the pathological neuronal dynamics with minimal intervention.
source: In theory, closed-loop stimulation guided by an efficient control algorithm should provide better outcomes, disrupting the pathological neuronal dynamics with minimal intervention.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on understanding of control systems.

claim: It is very challenging to foresee what type of control algorithms would be effective for neuronal systems.
source: But, given the complexity of neuronal systems, it is very challenging to foresee what type of control algorithms would be effective.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known complexity of neuronal systems.

claim: Multiple in silico studies focused on employing closed-loop control methods to desynchronise pathological oscillations in computational models of neurological disorders.
source: Multiple in silico studies focused on employing closed-loop control methods to desynchronise pathological oscillations in computational models of neurological disorders (Beverlin Ii and Netoff, 2012; Holt et al., 2016; Nabi et al., 2013; Weerasinghe et al., 2021; Witt et al., 2013), but these have not been translated into studies with real neuronal systems to access its viability.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior computational studies.

claim: In silico studies on closed-loop control have not been translated into studies with real neuronal systems.
source: Multiple in silico studies focused on employing closed-loop control methods to desynchronise pathological oscillations in computational models of neurological disorders (Beverlin Ii and Netoff, 2012; Holt et al., 2016; Nabi et al., 2013; Weerasinghe et al., 2021; Witt et al., 2013), but these have not been translated into studies with real neuronal systems to access its viability.
evidence: This establishes a gap in the literature that the current work addresses.

claim: DFC is a technique from chaos theory developed to stabilise/destabilise chaotic systems using minimal perturbations.
source: A particularly prevalent method in the field is delayed feedback control (DFC), a technique from chaos theory developed to stabilise/destabilise chaotic systems using minimal perturbations (Pyragas, 1992; Rosenblum and Pikovsky, 2004a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work on DFC.

claim: DFC controls the system by applying a feedback signal proportional to the difference between the current oscillation amplitude and the oscillation amplitude from a fixed delay into the past.
source: DFC controls the system by applying a feedback signal proportional to the difference between the current oscillation amplitude and the oscillation amplitude from a fixed delay into the past.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of DFC as implemented in the study.

claim: DFC has been extensively applied in the context of in silico neuroscience, with studies focusing on specific disorders such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy.
source: DFC has been extensively applied in the context of in silico neuroscience, with studies focusing on specific disorders such as Parkinson's disease (Rosenblum and Pikovsky, 2004b; Vlachos et al., 2016; Popovych et al., 2017; Daneshzand et al., 2018; Popovych and Tass, 2019; Yu et al., 2021) and epilepsy (Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior computational studies.

claim: There is controversy in the literature regarding DFC efficacy and whether it may instead promote synchronisation, depending on the baseline levels of synchrony of the modelled network.
source: However, there is still controversy in the literature regarding its efficacy and whether it may instead promote synchronisation, depending on the baseline levels of synchrony of the modelled network (Dovzhenok et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dovzhenok et al., 2013.

claim: It is critical to test the effectiveness of DFC with biological neuronal networks that display synchronised oscillatory firing.
source: Thus, it is critical to test the effectiveness of DFC with biological neuronal networks that display synchronised oscillatory firing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the controversy in the literature and the need for experimental validation.

claim: Neuronal cultures on microelectrode arrays (MEAs) are a useful testbed for testing DFC.
source: Neuronal cultures on microelectrode arrays (MEAs) are a useful testbed for this task: these cultures self-organise into complex interconnected networks with quasiperiodic synchronised bursting, and MEAs enable closed-loop modulation of the neuronal activity, providing concurrent recording and stimulation at multiple points of the population with high spatial and temporal resolution (Obien et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and describes the experimental platform used.

claim: Neuronal cultures on MEAs self-organise into complex interconnected networks with quasiperiodic synchronised bursting.
source: Neuronal cultures on microelectrode arrays (MEAs) are a useful testbed for this task: these cultures self-organise into complex interconnected networks with quasiperiodic synchronised bursting, and MEAs enable closed-loop modulation of the neuronal activity, providing concurrent recording and stimulation at multiple points of the population with high spatial and temporal resolution (Obien et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes a known property of neuronal cultures on MEAs.

claim: MEAs enable closed-loop modulation of neuronal activity with high spatial and temporal resolution.
source: Neuronal cultures on microelectrode arrays (MEAs) are a useful testbed for this task: these cultures self-organise into complex interconnected networks with quasiperiodic synchronised bursting, and MEAs enable closed-loop modulation of the neuronal activity, providing concurrent recording and stimulation at multiple points of the population with high spatial and temporal resolution (Obien et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation describing MEA capabilities.

claim: Traditional DFC lacks the adaptability to cope with the malleable dynamics of biological networks.
source: We show that traditional DFC lacks the adaptability to cope with the malleable dynamics of biological networks and may actually impose a new firing periodicity.
evidence: This is a key finding from the experimental data.

claim: Traditional DFC may actually impose a new firing periodicity.
source: We show that traditional DFC lacks the adaptability to cope with the malleable dynamics of biological networks and may actually impose a new firing periodicity.
evidence: This is a key finding from the experimental data.

claim: aDFC reduces the synchronisation of the network.
source: We demonstrate that aDFC reduces the synchronisation of the network and efficiently disrupts the baseline oscillation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental results.

claim: aDFC efficiently disrupts the baseline oscillation.
source: We demonstrate that aDFC reduces the synchronisation of the network and efficiently disrupts the baseline oscillation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental results.

claim: The intrinsic firing dynamics of a network unveils its propensity for neuromodulation.
source: While doing so, we identified and characterised a new feature of biological neuronal networks: the intrinsic firing dynamics of a network unveils its propensity for neuromodulation.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Network controllability can be conditioned by specific parameters of the network architecture, such as the excitatory/inhibitory balance and overall synaptic weights of the network connections.
source: To better understand this relationship, we went back to the in silico neuronal networks and revealed that their controllability can be conditioned by specific parameters of the network architecture, such as the excitatory/inhibitory balance and overall synaptic weights of the network connections.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling work.

claim: Theoretical predictions regarding the efficacy of DFC might be misleading.
source: Taking all together, we show that theoretical predictions regarding the efficacy of DFC might be misleading and we present an improved algorithm for closed-loop electrical stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing in silico predictions with in vitro results.

claim: The in vitro setup provides a powerful testbed to analyse DFC algorithms.
source: Our in vitro setup provides a powerful testbed to analyse DFC algorithms as it incorporates neuronal populations that display synchronous oscillations (here in the form of quasiperiodic network bursts [NB] with periodicities in the seconds range), an acquisition system that measures the population's extracellular activity at high spatiotemporal resolution enabling the inference of synchrony among neurons, on-demand electrical pulse generators to stimulate the network at high spatiotemporal resolution, and a feedback loop with low actuation latency in the milliseconds range (orders of magnitude below that of the neuronal dynamics under control).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and its capabilities.

claim: The in vitro neuronal populations display synchronous oscillations in the form of quasiperiodic network bursts with periodicities in the seconds range.
source: Our in vitro setup provides a powerful testbed to analyse DFC algorithms as it incorporates neuronal populations that display synchronous oscillations (here in the form of quasiperiodic network bursts [NB] with periodicities in the seconds range), an acquisition system that measures the population's extracellular activity at high spatiotemporal resolution enabling the inference of synchrony among neurons, on-demand electrical pulse generators to stimulate the network at high spatiotemporal resolution, and a feedback loop with low actuation latency in the milliseconds range (orders of magnitude below that of the neuronal dynamics under control).
evidence: This describes the observed behavior of the neuronal cultures.

claim: The feedback loop has low actuation latency in the milliseconds range, orders of magnitude below that of the neuronal dynamics under control.
source: Our in vitro setup provides a powerful testbed to analyse DFC algorithms as it incorporates neuronal populations that display synchronous oscillations (here in the form of quasiperiodic network bursts [NB] with periodicities in the seconds range), an acquisition system that measures the population's extracellular activity at high spatiotemporal resolution enabling the inference of synchrony among neurons, on-demand electrical pulse generators to stimulate the network at high spatiotemporal resolution, and a feedback loop with low actuation latency in the milliseconds range (orders of magnitude below that of the neuronal dynamics under control).
evidence: This describes a technical specification of the experimental setup.

claim: When the activity is oscillatory, the actuation signal is maximal at the antiphase of the neuronal oscillation.
source: This way, when the activity is oscillatory, the actuation signal is maximal at the antiphase of the neuronal oscillation (Figure 1C, left and middle).
evidence: This describes the behavior of the DFC algorithm and is illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The actuation signal is explicitly dependent on the neuronal oscillation, so stimulation is highly activated when synchrony is high and decreases as this firing pattern vanishes.
source: Since the actuation signal is explicitly dependent on the neuronal oscillation, stimulation is highly activated when synchrony is high (Figure 1C, middle) and decreases as this firing pattern vanishes (Figure 1C, right).
evidence: This describes the behavior of the DFC algorithm and is illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: aDFC monitors the current periodicity of the neuronal oscillation and updates the delay duration and natural frequency of the oscillator accordingly.
source: This way, aDFC monitors the current periodicity of the neuronal oscillation (T) and updates the delay duration (T/2) and natural frequency of the oscillator (ω) accordingly (Figure 1B, blue and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the adaptive component of aDFC and is illustrated in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each experiment had three stages: 5 min of spontaneous activity pre-stimulation (OFF), 5 min under stimulation (ON), and 5 min of spontaneous activity post-stimulation (OFF).
source: Each experiment had three stages: 5 min of spontaneous activity pre-stimulation (OFF), 5 min under stimulation (ON), and 5 min of spontaneous activity post-stimulation (OFF).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Every network was submitted to three different stimulation algorithms: standard DFC, aDFC, and random stimulation.
source: Every network, here defined as a neuronal culture on a given day in vitro, was submitted to three different stimulation algorithms: standard DFC, aDFC, and random stimulation.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: During random stimulation, the electrical pulses were triggered by a Poisson process with an average frequency identical to that obtained in the preceding aDFC test.
source: During random stimulation, the electrical pulses were triggered by a Poisson process with an average frequency identical to that obtained in the preceding aDFC test.
evidence: This describes the control condition used in the experiments.

claim: In all algorithms, stimulation was provided as monophasic negative voltage pulses at controlled timings.
source: In all algorithms, stimulation was provided as monophasic negative voltage pulses at controlled timings.
evidence: This describes the stimulation parameters used.

claim: A single stimulation electrode was chosen that triggered a neuronal response measured by neighbouring electrodes, using the minimum voltage amplitude that achieved that response.
source: To ensure that the individual pulses had a comparable effect on the different neuronal networks, we chose a single stimulation electrode that triggered a neuronal response measured by neighbouring electrodes and the minimum voltage amplitude that achieved that response (see Methods section).
evidence: This describes the method for selecting stimulation parameters.

claim: DFC stimulation imposed a change to a faster and very consistent oscillation.
source: DFC stimulation imposed a change to a faster and very consistent oscillation (DFC periods in Figure 2A and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: DFC initially forces the network to fire in its antiphase, creating a change in the bursting periodicity.
source: This happens because DFC initially forces the network to fire in its antiphase, creating a change in the bursting periodicity.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed behavior of DFC.

claim: Since the change in bursting periodicity is not monitored to update the controller's delay, the delayed oscillator no longer matches the antiphase of the ongoing oscillation.
source: Since this change is not monitored to update the controller's delay, the delayed oscillator (Figure 1C, grey) no longer matches the antiphase of the ongoing oscillation.
evidence: This explains why DFC becomes ineffective or counterproductive.

claim: With DFC, stimulation becomes prejudicial as it is sent in phase with the new oscillation, reinforcing it.
source: Therefore, stimulation becomes prejudicial as it is sent in phase with the new oscillation, reinforcing it (DFC period in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an explanation for why DFC worsens oscillations, supported by Figure 2C.

claim: aDFC disrupts the spontaneous oscillation frequency exhibited by the network, creating a firing regime where there is no predominant oscillation.
source: On the other hand, aDFC disrupts the spontaneous oscillation frequency exhibited by the network, creating a firing regime where there is no predominant oscillation (aDFC periods in Figure 2B and E).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B and E.

claim: With aDFC, the controller is constantly forcing the network to fire in antiphase and aDFC adapts as the network oscillation changes with the stimulation.
source: In this case, the controller is constantly forcing the network to fire in antiphase and aDFC adapts as the network oscillation changes with the stimulation.
evidence: This explains the mechanism by which aDFC maintains effectiveness.

claim: The magnitude of the main oscillation was quantified by calculating the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the power spectrum density (PSD) of the instantaneous firing rate.
source: To quantify this effect, we calculated the magnitude of the main oscillation by calculating the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the power spectrum density (PSD) of the instantaneous firing rate for the ON and OFF segments (Figure 2D and F).
evidence: This describes the analysis method used, illustrated in Figure 2D and F.

claim: The effect of the different stimulation protocols was evaluated using three metrics: synchrony, firing rate, and oscillation intensity.
source: The effect of the different stimulation protocols was evaluated using three metrics calculated for the OFF and ON periods: synchrony, firing rate, and oscillation intensity.
evidence: This describes the analysis approach.

claim: Synchrony measures the degree of co-activation of multiple electrodes.
source: Synchrony measures the degree of co-activation of multiple electrodes (see Methods); firing rate corresponds to the average number of spikes per electrode per unit of time (not to be confused with the instantaneous network firing rate signal presented in Figure 2C and E); oscillation intensity corresponds to the SNR of the PSD of the instantaneous firing rate signal (Figure 2D and F).
evidence: This defines one of the metrics used in the analysis.

claim: Firing rate corresponds to the average number of spikes per electrode per unit of time.
source: Synchrony measures the degree of co-activation of multiple electrodes (see Methods); firing rate corresponds to the average number of spikes per electrode per unit of time (not to be confused with the instantaneous network firing rate signal presented in Figure 2C and E); oscillation intensity corresponds to the SNR of the PSD of the instantaneous firing rate signal (Figure 2D and F).
evidence: This defines one of the metrics used in the analysis.

claim: Oscillation intensity corresponds to the SNR of the PSD of the instantaneous firing rate signal.
source: Synchrony measures the degree of co-activation of multiple electrodes (see Methods); firing rate corresponds to the average number of spikes per electrode per unit of time (not to be confused with the instantaneous network firing rate signal presented in Figure 2C and E); oscillation intensity corresponds to the SNR of the PSD of the instantaneous firing rate signal (Figure 2D and F).
evidence: This defines one of the metrics used in the analysis.

claim: Some networks were consistently driven to distinct regions of the features space with each stimulation protocol.
source: Some networks were consistently driven to distinct regions of the features space with each stimulation protocol (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Controllable networks are those that can hypothetically be led to any desired reachable state by an ideal controller.
source: We refer to these as controllable networks – hypothetically, an ideal controller could lead such networks to any desired reachable state.
evidence: This defines the concept of controllable networks used in the study.

claim: Some networks did not exhibit consistent modulation when stimulated using the different protocols.
source: On the other hand, some networks did not exhibit consistent modulation when stimulated using the different protocols (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Uncontrollable networks are those that did not exhibit consistent modulation when stimulated.
source: We termed these uncontrollable networks.
evidence: This defines the concept of uncontrollable networks used in the study.

claim: Each network was classified as either controllable or uncontrollable by calculating the multivariate ANOVA (MANOVA) for the ON values of the three metrics.
source: Based on this definition, each network was classified as either controllable or uncontrollable by calculating the multivariate ANOVA (MANOVA) for the ON values of the three metrics (see Methods for details).
evidence: This describes the statistical method used for classification.

claim: Networks with low p-values (p<0.05) were considered controllable.
source: Networks with low p-values (p<0.05) (i.e. networks with significantly distinct neuromodulation results for the different stimulation protocols) were considered controllable (Figure 3D).
evidence: This describes the criterion for classifying networks as controllable.

claim: Controllability of a network is dependent on the assumed stimulation configuration.
source: Conceptually, controllability of a network is dependent on the assumed stimulation configuration: a network may be controllable with an array of stimulating electrodes, and uncontrollable using a single stimulating electrode.
evidence: This is a conceptual point about the definition of controllability.

claim: Controllable and uncontrollable networks lie in different regions of the feature space defined by spontaneous firing rate and synchrony.
source: This revealed that, as hypothesised, controllable and uncontrollable networks lie in different regions of the feature space (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Controllable networks are in the center of the feature space, associated with intermediate levels of spontaneous firing rate and synchrony.
source: Furthermore, controllable networks are in the centre, which is associated with intermediate levels of spontaneous firing rate and synchrony.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The experiments performed with controllable networks are in the centre of the principal component distribution, surrounded by a bimodal distribution of the experiments performed with uncontrollable networks.
source: A histogram shows that the experiments performed with controllable networks are in the centre, surrounded by a bimodal distribution of the experiments performed with uncontrollable networks (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a finding from the principal component analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Both aDFC and random stimulation led to a significant decrease in oscillation intensity.
source: Both aDFC and random stimulation led to a significant decrease in oscillation intensity (see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for a representative wavelet transform under Poisson stimulation).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The standard DFC algorithm led to a significant increase in the oscillations.
source: The standard DFC algorithm, on the other hand, led to a significant increase in the oscillations.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The increase in oscillation magnitude with DFC was followed by an increase in the oscillation frequency.
source: This increase in magnitude was followed by an increase in the oscillation frequency (Figure 2A, C and D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: aDFC was the only stimulation protocol that led to a significant decrease in synchrony.
source: The only stimulation protocol that led to a significant decrease in synchrony was aDFC (Figure 4B) and its effect was significantly different from that of random stimulation.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: aDFC was the only method that significantly increased the average firing rate.
source: On the other hand, it was also the only method that significantly increased the average firing rate (Figure 4D), even though the average stimulation frequency was similar for the three methods (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The average stimulation frequency was similar for the three methods (aDFC, DFC, and Poisson).
source: On the other hand, it was also the only method that significantly increased the average firing rate (Figure 4D), even though the average stimulation frequency was similar for the three methods (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In silico networks were modeled as randomly connected networks of 1000 Izhikevich neurons with different proportions of regular spiking excitatory neurons and fast-spiking inhibitory neurons.
source: We modelled randomly connected networks of 1000 Izhikevich neurons (Izhikevich, 2003) with different proportions of regular spiking excitatory neurons and fast-spiking inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This describes the computational model used.

claim: The overall synaptic weight was varied in the in silico simulations.
source: We also varied the overall synaptic weight (see Methods for details).
evidence: This describes a parameter varied in the computational model.

claim: Each simulation condition was simulated five times.
source: Each condition was simulated five times.
evidence: This describes the computational experimental design.

claim: The simulations were composed of two different periods: spontaneous activity (OFF) and controlled activity (aDFC ON).
source: The simulations were composed of two different periods: spontaneous activity (OFF) and controlled activity (aDFC ON).
evidence: This describes the computational experimental protocol.

claim: Low percentages of excitatory neurons and weak synaptic weights within the network led to sparse and chaotic activity.
source: Low percentages of excitatory neurons and weak synaptic weights within the network led to sparse and chaotic activity (region 1 in Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: In sparse and chaotic activity regimes, the controller is sporadically activated due to fluctuations of neuronal activity, creating brief moments of synchronisation.
source: In this scenario, the controller is sporadically activated due to fluctuations of neuronal activity, creating brief moments of synchronisation (Figure 5C, top).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational simulations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: High percentages of excitatory neurons and strong synaptic weights led to highly ordered network dynamics with strong bursting activity.
source: High percentages of excitatory neurons and strong synaptic weights led to highly ordered network dynamics with strong bursting activity (region 3 in Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: In highly ordered network dynamics with strong bursting, the controller could not disrupt the dominating spontaneous activity.
source: Here, the controller could not disrupt the dominating spontaneous activity (Figure 5C, bottom).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational simulations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the transition between sparse/chaotic and highly ordered network states, there was a parameter subspace that generated intermediate baseline levels of firing rate and synchrony.
source: However, in the transition between these two network states, there was a parameter subspace that generated intermediate baseline levels of firing rate and synchrony (region 2 in Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the intermediate parameter region, the networks were controllable, parallel to what was found in vitro.
source: In parallel to what was found in vitro, the networks were controllable in this intermediate region (see also Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational simulations that parallels the in vitro results.

claim: In the intermediate parameter region, aDFC could desynchronise the network shortly after activating the stimulation.
source: Here, aDFC could desynchronise the network shortly after activating the stimulation (Figure 5C, middle).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational simulations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Among the multiple possible parameters governing network controllability, the excitatory/inhibitory balance and overall network connectivity strength could explain the separation into controllable and uncontrollable networks seen in vitro.
source: Thus, among the multiple possible parameters governing network controllability, the excitatory/inhibitory balance and overall network connectivity strength could explain the separation into controllable and uncontrollable networks seen in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling results.

claim: The majority of the in vitro cultures had monostable dynamics, presenting a very consistent firing pattern over time.
source: The majority of the in vitro cultures had monostable dynamics, presenting a very consistent firing pattern over time (e.g. OFF periods of Figure 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: In monostable networks, aDFC reduced neuronal synchronisation and disrupted baseline oscillatory activity, but generally did so by creating sparser bursting with no particular periodicity.
source: In these networks, even though aDFC reduced neuronal synchronisation (Figure 4C) and disrupted baseline oscillatory activity (Figure 2B, E and F and Figure 4A), it generally did so by creating sparser bursting with no particular periodicity.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: In monostable networks, aDFC did not promote a phase transition to a stable asynchronous state (AS).
source: In monostable networks, aDFC did not promote a phase transition to a stable asynchronous state (AS) as opposed to what is typically seen in DFC computational studies (Rosenblum and Pikovsky, 2004a; Vlachos et al., 2016; Popovych et al., 2017; Daneshzand et al., 2018; Popovych and Tass, 2019; Yu et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, contrasted with computational studies.

claim: Some networks had multi-stable dynamics, spontaneously transitioning between different firing regimes.
source: We also found a less common type of networks that had multi-stable dynamics, spontaneously transitioning between different firing regimes.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Multi-stable networks were particularly interesting when they presented sporadic transitions to an AS, showing that these networks could autonomously sustain asynchronous activity.
source: Multi-stable networks were particularly interesting when they presented sporadic transitions to an AS as it showed that these networks could autonomously sustain asynchronous activity, even if only for short periods of time (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The different stable states were identified using unsupervised clustering on the values of firing rate and synchrony calculated over a sliding window.
source: The different stable states were identified using unsupervised clustering on the values of firing rate and synchrony calculated over a sliding window (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This describes the analysis method used, illustrated in Figure 6A and B.

claim: A given state was considered asynchronous if its average synchrony was below 0.5 and the mean firing rate was below the average of that network.
source: A given state was considered asynchronous if its average synchrony was below 0.5 and the mean firing rate was below the average of that network.
evidence: This defines the criterion for identifying asynchronous states.

claim: The obtained clusters correlate with the different regimes seen in the frequency domain.
source: The obtained clusters correlate with the different regimes seen in the frequency domain (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: One multi-stable network presented the required criteria to evaluate the effectiveness of stimulation protocols in promoting transitions to AS.
source: Out of all the networks tested, one presented the required criteria to evaluate this effect (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This describes the sample available for this specific analysis.

claim: aDFC consistently promoted desynchronisation in all the trials performed with the multi-stable network, leading to a considerable increase of time spent in AS.
source: aDFC consistently promoted desynchronisation in all the trials performed with this network, leading to a considerable increase of time spent in AS (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: DFC stimulation tended to impose a new bursting periodicity, sometimes interrupted by transitions to AS.
source: DFC stimulation, on the other hand, tended to impose a new bursting periodicity (as already reported), sometimes interrupted by transitions to AS (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: The percentage of time spent in AS during DFC stimulation is within the range of spontaneous transitions and thus cannot be directly attributed to DFC.
source: However, the percentage of time spent in AS during DFC stimulation is within the range of spontaneous transitions and thus cannot be directly attributed to DFC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Random Poisson stimulation with identical stimulation frequency promoted sparser bursting with some transitions to AS, but these are also within the range of spontaneous transitions.
source: Random Poisson stimulation with identical stimulation frequency promoted sparser bursting with some transitions to AS, but these are also within the range of spontaneous transitions (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 7G and H.

claim: The precisely timed stimuli determined by aDFC are causing the transitions to the AS.
source: This means that the precisely timed stimuli determined by aDFC are causing the transitions to the AS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing aDFC to random stimulation.

claim: Random Poisson stimulation, being an open-loop protocol, does not stop once the desired AS is achieved, which could be a significant drawback in a clinical setting.
source: Also, the random Poisson stimulation, being an open-loop protocol, does not stop once the desired AS is achieved, which could be a significant drawback in a clinical setting.
evidence: This is an inference about the clinical implications of open-loop vs closed-loop control.

claim: Controlling brain activity is a long-standing goal in neuroengineering and holds great potential for multiple clinical applications.
source: Controlling brain activity is a long-standing goal in neuroengineering and holds great potential for multiple clinical applications.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field.

claim: Controlling brain activity is challenging because neuronal systems have complex dynamics, virtually impossible to fully observe, and the space of actions available to an external controller is highly restricted.
source: This is a challenging problem because neuronal systems have complex dynamics, virtually impossible to fully observe, and the space of actions available to an external controller is highly restricted.
evidence: This explains why controlling brain activity is difficult.

claim: Most constraints in controlling neuronal systems are circumvented in computational studies, allowing researchers to explore solutions in a highly controlled environment.
source: Most of these constraints are circumvented in computational studies, allowing researchers to explore solutions in a highly controlled environment.
evidence: This describes the advantages of computational studies.

claim: Under simplified conditions, computational solutions may converge to algorithms that fail when applied to biological neuronal populations.
source: However, under such simplified conditions, these solutions may converge to algorithms that fail when applied to biological neuronal populations.
evidence: This is a concern about the limitations of computational studies.

claim: It is important to assess the performance of control algorithms with simple biological neuronal systems before moving to in vivo trials.
source: It is, therefore, important to assess the performance of such algorithms with simple biological neuronal systems before moving to in vivo trials.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation based on the limitations of computational studies.

claim: This work tested the efficacy of conventional DFC in an in vitro setting for the first time.
source: In this work, we tested, for the first time, the efficacy of conventional DFC in an in vitro setting and reported that it promoted a new bursting frequency, instead of ablating it.
evidence: This establishes the novelty of the experimental work.

claim: Conventional DFC promoted a new bursting frequency instead of ablating it.
source: In this work, we tested, for the first time, the efficacy of conventional DFC in an in vitro setting and reported that it promoted a new bursting frequency, instead of ablating it.
evidence: This is a key finding from the experimental data.

claim: The finding that DFC promotes a new bursting frequency is in line with the claim that linear DFC could lead to synchronisation if the delay deviated substantially from the half-period.
source: This is in line with the claim that linear DFC could lead to synchronisation if the delay deviated substantially from the half-period (Pyragas, 2006).
evidence: This connects the experimental finding to prior theoretical work.

claim: In prior computational studies, the deviation from the half-period delay was tested by varying delays with the same network.
source: This was shown in silico by testing different delays with the same network.
evidence: This describes how the phenomenon was studied in prior computational work.

claim: In this work, the deviation from the half-period delay was caused by the fact that DFC stimulation induced a faster periodicity, while the delay was kept constant.
source: Here, however, the deviation from the half-period delay was caused by the fact that DFC stimulation induced a faster periodicity, while the delay was kept constant.
evidence: This explains the mechanism by which DFC failed in the biological system.

claim: The neuronal dynamics aligned with the non-adaptive controller to the point that almost all activity was confined to stimulus responses.
source: The neuronal dynamics aligned with the non-adaptive controller to the point that almost all activity was confined to stimulus responses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The failure mode of DFC was not predicted by computational studies, possibly because the simple in silico networks used were not as dynamic as biological ones.
source: This was not predicted by computational studies, possibly because the simple in silico networks used were not as dynamic as biological ones and, therefore, could not sustain different synchronisation periodicities.
evidence: This is a speculation about why computational studies did not predict the observed behavior.

claim: Random stimulation, using similar stimulation frequency to aDFC, was able to disrupt oscillations, although without significantly decreasing synchronisation.
source: Interestingly, random stimulation, using similar stimulation frequency, was also able to achieve this, although without significantly decreasing synchronisation.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Electrical stimulation may be acting as a disrupter of the network dynamics, as has been proposed for high-frequency deep brain stimulation.
source: Electrical stimulation may be acting as a disrupter of the network dynamics, as it has been proposed for high-frequency deep brain stimulation (Chiken and Nambu, 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of action, supported by a citation.

claim: Not all networks could be effectively modulated by each stimulation protocol.
source: We showed that not all networks could be effectively modulated by each stimulation protocol.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Controllability is contingent on the neurostimulation conditions.
source: However, it is important to note that controllability is contingent on the neurostimulation conditions.
evidence: This is a conceptual point about the definition of controllability.

claim: The fact that only one stimulating electrode was used may restrict the pool of controllable networks.
source: In particular, the fact that we only used one stimulating electrode may restrict the pool of controllable networks.
evidence: This is a speculation about a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: Using one stimulating electrode follows the principle that DFC should control the system using minimal intervention.
source: We did so to follow the principle that DFC should control the system using minimal intervention (Rosenblum and Pikovsky, 2004a).
evidence: This explains the rationale for the experimental design choice.

claim: Despite aDFC decreasing the synchrony of controllable networks, the neuronal activity was still mostly dominated by synchronous events.
source: Also, despite the fact that aDFC decreased the synchrony of controllable networks, the neuronal activity was still mostly dominated by synchronous events.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The results were far from those obtained in previous in silico studies, where the synchronous events vanish almost completely.
source: These results were far from those obtained in previous in silico studies, where the synchronous events vanish almost completely.
evidence: This compares the experimental results to prior computational studies.

claim: With the experimental setup, only excitatory electrical stimulation could be applied, much like existing implantable stimulators.
source: First, with our setup, we could only apply excitatory electrical stimulation, much like existing implantable stimulators.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the experimental setup.

claim: When the actuation signal was negative, no input was sent to the network.
source: For this reason, when the actuation signal (here modulated as a stimulation frequency) was negative, we sent no input to the network.
evidence: This describes how the control algorithm was implemented given the hardware constraints.

claim: In theory, using only the positive phase of the actuation signal should still prevent the formation of synchronous events, as it did in in silico tests.
source: Nonetheless, in theory, using only the positive phase of the actuation signal should still prevent the formation of synchronous events, as it did in our in silico tests.
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on computational modeling.

claim: It is possible that the limiting factor is the neuronal model itself.
source: So, it is possible that the limiting factor is the neuronal model itself.
evidence: This is a speculation about why the experimental results differed from computational predictions.

claim: The unconstrained growth of hippocampal cultures may have led to highly interconnected networks whose neurons simply cannot fire asynchronously.
source: The unconstrained growth of our hippocampal cultures may have led to highly interconnected networks whose neurons simply cannot fire asynchronously.
evidence: This is a speculation about a property of the biological networks that may limit controllability.

claim: The speculation about network connectivity is supported by the fact that aDFC consistently promoted the AS in a network that could already sustain it autonomously.
source: This is further supported by the fact that aDFC consistently promoted the AS in a network that could already sustain it autonomously.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation with the multi-stable network.

claim: Other methods can achieve network desynchronisation by following approaches that are more aggressive.
source: Other methods can achieve network desynchronisation by following approaches that are more aggressive.
evidence: This acknowledges alternative approaches in the literature.

claim: Continuous stimulation at higher frequencies (10–50 Hz), distributed across multiple electrodes, can prevent network synchronisation.
source: Namely, it was already shown that continuous stimulation at higher frequencies (10–50 Hz), distributed across multiple electrodes, can prevent network synchronisation (Wagenaar et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: High-frequency stimulation prevents synchronisation at the cost of highly increasing the overall network's firing rate, thus possibly establishing yet another non-physiological state.
source: This is done, however, at the cost of highly increasing the overall network's firing rate, thus possibly establishing yet another non-physiological state.
evidence: This is a concern about the side effects of high-frequency stimulation.

claim: The goal of avoiding an abnormal prolonged increase in the population's firing rate is grounded on the understanding that excessive activity is also detrimental in a neuronal circuit.
source: The goal of avoiding an abnormal prolonged increase in the population's firing rate is grounded on the understanding that excessive activity is also detrimental in a neuronal circuit.
evidence: This is a rationale based on neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Whether aDFC is more efficient in disrupting pathological oscillations than high-frequency stimulation (HFS) used in current stimulation therapies remains unknown.
source: Whether aDFC is more efficient in disrupting pathological oscillations than high-frequency stimulation (HFS) used in current stimulation therapies remains unknown.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the current study.

claim: As opposed to fixed/continuous HFS, aDFC stimulation adapts to the population oscillation frequency and ceases once the network is desynchronised.
source: Nevertheless, as opposed to fixed/continuous HFS, aDFC stimulation adapts to the population oscillation frequency and ceases once the network is desynchronised.
evidence: This highlights an advantage of aDFC over HFS.

claim: There is still margin to improve the aDFC algorithm by making it self-adaptive in terms of the actuation gain, pulse amplitude, and selection of stimulation electrode(s).
source: Despite being able to disrupt the baseline oscillation and decreasing synchrony levels, there is still margin to improve the aDFC algorithm by making it self-adaptive in terms of the actuation gain, pulse amplitude, and selection of stimulation electrode(s), all of which were tuned manually before starting the experiments.
evidence: This suggests future directions for improving the algorithm.

claim: It remains to be explored whether a fully adaptive controller would consistently achieve full desynchronisation in these types of networks.
source: It remains to be explored whether such an adaptive controller would consistently achieve full desynchronisation in this type of networks.
evidence: This identifies an open question for future research.

claim: Technological advances in implantable neurostimulators open the door for the use of algorithms capable of controlling pathological neuronal dynamics.
source: To conclude, the technological advances made in implantable neurostimulators open the door for the use of algorithms capable of controlling pathological neuronal dynamics.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field and its potential.

claim: aDFC has the potential to be a promising candidate for therapeutic closed-loop brain stimulation.
source: We show that aDFC has the potential to be a promising candidate and believe that the considerations extracted from this in vitro study will support the translation to future in vivo experiments.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The considerations extracted from this in vitro study will support the translation to future in vivo experiments.
source: We show that aDFC has the potential to be a promising candidate and believe that the considerations extracted from this in vitro study will support the translation to future in vivo experiments.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about the impact of the work.

claim: Embryonic (E18) rat hippocampal neurons were cultured on six-well or nine-well chamber MEA with specified densities.
source: Embryonic (E18) rat hippocampal neurons were cultured on six-well or nine-well chamber MEA (256-6well MEA200/30iR-ITO-rcr and 256-9wellMEA300/30iR-ITO, respectively) (MCS, Germany) with a density of 5×104 cells/well and 3×104 cells/well, respectively.
evidence: This describes the cell culture methods used.

claim: The experiments were performed between 13 and 55 days in vitro.
source: The experiments were performed between 13 and 55 days in vitro.
evidence: This describes the timing of the experiments.

claim: The recordings were performed with the MEA2100-256 System.
source: The recordings were performed with the MEA2100-256 System (MCS, Germany).
evidence: This describes the recording equipment used.

claim: The electrophysiology signals were sampled at 10 kHz and filtered with a high-pass filter at 200 Hz.
source: The electrophysiology signals were sampled at 10 kHz and filtered with an HP at 200 Hz (second-order high-pass Butterworth filter).
evidence: This describes the signal processing parameters.

claim: Neuronal spikes were detected when peaks were six STD (sometimes up to eight STD) below or above baseline.
source: The neuronal spikes were detected and recorded using the Experimenter software from MCS. Peaks that were six STD (sometimes up to eight STD, depending on the background noise) below or above baseline were considered neuronal spikes.
evidence: This describes the spike detection method.

claim: There was a deadtime of 3 ms after each spike detection to prevent biphasic spikes from being identified twice.
source: There was a deadtime of 3 ms after each detection to prevent biphasic spikes from being identified twice.
evidence: This describes a technical detail of the spike detection method.

claim: The developed C# software was built using the McsUsbNet dynamic link library from MCS.
source: The developed C# software was built using the McsUsbNet dynamic link library from MCS (https://github.com/multichannelsystems/McsUsbNet; Multi Channel Systems MCS GmbH, 2023).
evidence: This describes the software development.

claim: The overall closed-loop latency associated with the activation of the stimulus was below 40 ms.
source: The overall closed-loop latency associated with the activation of the stimulus was below 40 ms.
evidence: This describes a technical specification of the closed-loop system.

claim: The application monitored only electrodes that had an average firing rate above 0.1 Hz.
source: The application only monitored electrodes that had an average firing rate of above 0.1 Hz, measured before starting the experiments.
evidence: This describes a parameter of the control algorithm.

claim: The instantaneous firing rate (FR) of an active electrode was calculated in a square moving window of 0.1 s.
source: The instantaneous firing rate (FR) of an active electrode was calculated in a square moving window of 0.1 s (sometimes tuned to 0.2 or 0.5 before starting the experiments depending on the dynamics of the network).
evidence: This describes a parameter of the control algorithm.

claim: Each stimulus unit was a negative electrical pulse with 200 µs duration.
source: Each stimulus unit was a negative electrical pulse with 200 µs duration.
evidence: This describes the stimulation parameters.

claim: The choice of stimulation electrode and pulse amplitude was based on the premise that the stimulus should promote a response in the neighbouring electrodes using minimal stimulation.
source: The choice of stimulation electrode and pulse amplitude was based on the premise that the stimulus should promote a response in the neighbouring electrodes using minimal stimulation.
evidence: This describes the rationale for selecting stimulation parameters.

claim: Different electrodes were probed manually using Experimenter software, starting with the most active ones.
source: We probed different electrodes manually using Experimenter software, starting with the most active ones.
evidence: This describes the method for selecting the stimulation electrode.

claim: For each electrode, different stimulus amplitudes from –400 to –1000 mV in steps of –100 mV were tested.
source: For each electrode, we tested different stimulus amplitudes from –400 to –1000 mV in steps of –100 mV.
evidence: This describes the method for selecting the stimulation amplitude.

claim: When a given electrode and stimulation amplitude evoked a consistent response, the stimulus amplitude was fixed to 120% of that value.
source: When a given electrode and stimulation amplitude evoked a consistent response in nearby neurons, we fixed the stimulus amplitude to 120% of that value to account for eventual adaptations of the network, which could render the stimulation ineffective.
evidence: This describes the method for setting the final stimulation amplitude.

claim: The experiments started with a recording of 15 min of spontaneous activity.
source: The experiments started with a recording of 15 min of spontaneous activity.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: The choice of stimulation protocols for the trials was randomised.
source: The choice of stimulation protocols – DFC, aDFC, and Poisson – for the following trials was randomised.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The time interval between consecutive trials was in the order of 5 min.
source: The time interval between consecutive trials was in the order of 5 min.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: A precise time interval between trials was not required because, once stimulation stopped, the firing dynamics returned to the baseline regime very quickly.
source: A precise time interval between trials was not required/imposed as, once stimulation stopped, the firing dynamics returned to the baseline regime very quickly (Figure 2A and B and Figure 3A).
evidence: This explains why a precise inter-trial interval was not necessary, supported by figures.

claim: Experiments were only performed on networks that displayed consistent oscillatory bursting activity with periodicities between 0.5 and 5 s.
source: We only performed experiments on networks that displayed consistent oscillatory bursting activity with periodicities between 0.5 and 5 s, approximately.
evidence: This describes the selection criteria for networks.

claim: Some cultures were rejected because they were (or became) irresponsive to stimulation.
source: Some cultures presented the required dynamics but were rejected because they were (or became) irresponsive to stimulation.
evidence: This describes an exclusion criterion.

claim: Only networks that were submitted to at least three trials with each protocol were analysed.
source: In order to have statistical robustness in the evaluation of the different stimulation protocols, we only analysed networks that were submitted to at least three trials with each protocol.
evidence: This describes an inclusion criterion for analysis.

claim: A total of 14 networks fulfilled the criteria to proceed with the experiments and analysis.
source: A total of 14 networks fulfilled the criteria to proceed with the experiments and analysis.
evidence: This describes the sample size.

claim: A network is defined as a neuronal culture in a given day in vitro.
source: Here, we define a network as being a neuronal culture in a given day in vitro.
evidence: This defines a key term used in the study.

claim: The neuronal dynamics of the same culture of neurons may change drastically from day to day, so it was considered a different dynamical system.
source: We did this because the neuronal dynamics of the same culture of neurons may change drastically from day to day, so we considered it a different dynamical system.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the definition of a network.

claim: The 14 networks came from 11 independent cultures, from a total of five different animal preparations.
source: The 14 networks came from 11 independent cultures, from a total of five different animal preparations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the sample composition.

claim: The synchrony measure is based on the χ metric, which compares the variance of the network activity with the variance of each neuron's activity.
source: The synchrony measure is based on the χ metric, which compares the variance of the network activity with the variance of each neuron's activity (Golomb and Rinzel, 1994),
evidence: This describes the synchrony metric used, with a citation.

claim: The synchrony metric measures the degree of co-activation of the multiple electrodes, regardless of the number of spikes exhibited by different electrodes at the moment of synchronisation.
source: We are thus measuring the degree of co-activation of the multiple electrodes, regardless of the number spikes exhibited by different electrodes at the moment of synchronisation.
evidence: This explains what the synchrony metric captures.

claim: The oscillation intensity is measured by calculating SNR of fundamental frequency of the PSD.
source: The oscillation intensity is measured by calculating SNR of fundamental frequency of the PSD.
evidence: This describes the oscillation intensity metric.

claim: For the firing rate and synchrony, the effect of each stimulation protocol was evaluated by calculating the metric's fold change from OFF to ON.
source: For the firing rate and synchrony, the effect of each stimulation protocol was evaluated by calculating the metric's fold change from OFF to ON.
evidence: This describes the analysis method.

claim: For the oscillation intensity, the difference between the OFF and ON periods was calculated, since it is measured in dB.
source: For the oscillation intensity we calculated the difference between the OFF and ON periods, since it is measured in dB, which is a logarithmic scale.
evidence: This describes the analysis method for oscillation intensity.

claim: The different states of neuronal activity were identified by calculating the firing rate and synchrony in a moving window.
source: The different states of neuronal activity of a given recording (Figure 6) were identified by calculating the firing rate and synchrony in a moving window.
evidence: This describes the method for identifying different activity states.

claim: The width of the moving window corresponded to the average duration of five periodic events in the analysed recording.
source: The width of the moving window corresponded to the average duration of five periodic events in the analysed recording.
evidence: This describes a parameter of the analysis method.

claim: The moving step was half the window width.
source: The moving step was half the window width.
evidence: This describes a parameter of the analysis method.

claim: The clusters of neuronal dynamics were automatically identified with Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) applied to the bidimensional matrix of firing rate and synchrony.
source: The clusters of neuronal dynamics were automatically identified with Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) applied to the bidimensional matrix of firing rate and synchrony.
evidence: This describes the clustering method used.

claim: GMMs with one to four groups were tested and each condition was repeated 10 times with different initial values.
source: We tested GMMs with one to four groups and each condition was repeated 10 times with different initial values.
evidence: This describes the clustering procedure.

claim: The ideal clustering was chosen based on the Bayesian informative criterion.
source: The ideal clustering was chosen based on the Bayesian informative criterion.
evidence: This describes the method for selecting the best clustering.

claim: The classification of networks as controllable or uncontrollable was based on the assumption that controllable networks could be driven to specific subspaces of neuronal activity with a given stimulation protocol.
source: The classification of networks as controllable or uncontrollable (Figure 3) was based on the assumption that controllable networks could be driven to specific subspaces of neuronal activity with a given stimulation protocol whereas the uncontrollable networks could not.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the classification method.

claim: MANOVA was calculated considering the fold change of the three metrics simultaneously to evaluate whether the spaces reached during stimulation were statistically different.
source: To evaluate whether the spaces reached during stimulation were statistically different, we calculated the MANOVA considering the fold change of the three metrics, simultaneously.
evidence: This describes the statistical test used.

claim: The null hypothesis for the MANOVA was that the modulation results were identical for all stimulation protocols.
source: Here, the null hypothesis was that the modulation results were identical for all stimulation protocols.
evidence: This describes the null hypothesis for the statistical test.

claim: For a given network, the average fold change in synchrony and firing rate, and the difference in SNR of the main oscillation were calculated across all trials performed with each stimulation protocol.
source: For a given network, we calculated the average fold change in synchrony and firing rate, and the difference in SNR of the main oscillation across all the trials performed with each stimulation protocol.
evidence: This describes the analysis method for comparing protocols.

claim: Comparisons between groups were performed using one-way ANOVA with repeated measures.
source: Then, the comparisons between groups were performed using one-way ANOVA with repeated measures.
evidence: This describes the statistical test used.

claim: To compare the efficacy of different stimulation protocols in promoting transition to AS, the percentage of time spent in AS during OFF and ON periods was calculated for all trials.
source: To compare the efficacy of the different stimulation protocols in promoting the transition to a stable AS in a multi-stable network, we calculated the percentage of time spent in the AS during the OFF and ON periods for all the trials.
evidence: This describes the analysis method for the multi-stable network.

claim: One-way ANOVA with repeated measures was used to compare if there was a significant change from OFF pre-stimulation to ON, from ON to OFF post-stimulation and from OFF pre-stimulation to OFF post-stimulation.
source: We then compared if there was a significant change from OFF pre-stimulation to ON, from ON to OFF post-stimulation and from OFF pre-stimulation to OFF post-stimulation using one-way ANOVA with repeated measures.
evidence: This describes the statistical test used for the multi-stable network analysis.

claim: The in silico model was based on the script provided in https://www.izhikevich.org/publications/net.m.
source: The model was based on the script provided in https://www.izhikevich.org/publications/net.m.
evidence: This describes the source of the computational model.

claim: The simulations had an initial period of 500 ms for the network activity to stabilise.
source: The simulations had an initial period of 500 ms for the network activity to stabilise.
evidence: This describes the simulation protocol.

claim: After the stabilisation period, there was 2000 ms of spontaneous activity and 2000 ms under the aDFC stimulation protocol.
source: After the stabilisation period, we had 2000 ms of spontaneous activity and 2000 ms under the aDFC stimulation protocol.
evidence: This describes the simulation protocol.

claim: The aDFC algorithm in simulations was identical to that applied in vitro, considering only the positive component of the actuation signal.
source: The aDFC algorithm was identical to that applied in vitro, considering only the positive component of the actuation signal.
evidence: This describes how the algorithm was implemented in simulations.

claim: A pool of 100 neurons was randomly selected for stimulation in the simulations.
source: A pool of 100 neurons was randomly selected for stimulation.
evidence: This describes the stimulation configuration in simulations.

claim: Each electrical pulse in the simulations corresponded to an instantaneous input of 20 mA to the stimulated neurons.
source: Each electrical pulse corresponded to an instantaneous input of 20 mA to the stimulated neurons.
evidence: This describes the stimulation parameters in simulations.

claim: The firing rate and synchrony measures in simulations were computed using the same algorithms as those used in vitro and averaged across the five repetitions of each simulation condition.
source: The firing rate and synchrony measures were computed using the same algorithms as those used in vitro (see Signal processing section) and averaged across the five repetitions of each simulation condition.
evidence: This describes the analysis method for the simulations.
